item.title: What Is Joe Manchin’s New Independent Leadership Council?
item.description: The council presents itself on its website as “an opportunity to fix politics.”

media:content.media:description: Then-Sen. Joe Manchin (I-WV) speaks to reporters outside the Senate Chamber on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on June 3, 2024.

item.content:encoded:
Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin is embarking on a new initiative: a project called the Independent Leadership Council.

The council—which the 78-year-old former senator is running with his daughter, Heather Manchin—will recruit and support independent candidates who are launching congressional bids. The former Senator launched the initiative at an event on Thursday, with several candidates in attendance, including California Rep. Kevin Kiley, who previously identified as a Republican but is now running a reelection campaign as an independent.

“We’re not trying to start another party,” Manchin told CNN in an interview that was published on Friday. “We’re trying to get a person who can be committed to—and totally committed to—being an independent with an independent voice. They can vote with Democrats and Republicans when they’re right and speak out against them when they’re wrong.”

The Manchins told CNN that if the council decides to support candidates, it will help them with campaigning, fundraising, and on-the-ground organizing. The Manchins were optimistic that, if their support can help a candidate win in the November midterms, then they might be able to have an impact on the 2028 presidential race.

“Our hope is that this is kind of our pilot, experiment, trying to prove it can be done,” Heather Manchin told CNN.

The council presents itself on its website as “an opportunity to fix politics.”

“America was founded on the belief that freedom and competition make us stronger. Somewhere along the way, our politics lost sight of those principles,” the website reads. “Decades of partisanship carved a divide most Americans never wanted. Instead of choosing sides, we’re changing the game by charting a new path that gives leaders the freedom to serve people, not parties.”

Manchin served in the Senate for more than a decade. For most of his political career, he was a centrist member of the Democratic Party. But he dropped that affiliation in 2024, shortly before the end of his time in the upper chamber, and re-registered as an independent. Even before he left the party, he frequently broke from his Democratic colleagues in his votes on various issues, including on climate change and tax hikes on the wealthy. He repeatedly criticized the Democratic Party, arguing that there wasn’t space for more conservative Democrats like him.

“Since becoming a United States senator in 2010, I have seen both the Democrat and Republican parties leave West Virginia and our country behind for partisan extremism while jeopardizing our democracy,” he said in a statement when he announced that he was switching his political affiliation. “Today, our national politics are broken and neither party is willing to compromise to find common ground. To stay true to myself and remain committed to put country before party, I have decided to register as an independent with no party affiliation and continue to fight for America’s sensible majority.”

Manchin’s renewed pushback against partisan politics now comes at a time when majorities of American adults “have an unfavorable view” of the Republican Party and Democratic Party, according to a Gallup poll released in May. And a record-high 45% of Americans identified as independents last year, Gallup polling released in January found.

item.title: How OpenAI Lost Control of an AI Model—and What Needs to Change
item.description: TIME spoke with experts and insiders about what must change to prevent the next AI escape.

media:content.media:description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman talks to reporters at the Dirksen Senate Office building in Washington, DC on June 3, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
OpenAI was evaluating its artificial intelligence models’ ability to exploit vulnerable software when instead the models hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, OpenAI revealed on July 21. Observers say this is the first real-world instance of AI doing something researchers have long worried about: a loss-of-control scenario. If the industry fails to learn from it, it is unlikely to be the last.

Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models and datasets, was the target of the autonomous attack, and reported the incident to local police before it knew OpenAI’s models were responsible. The breach was serious, but the immediate consequences were limited. Had similar behavior occurred inside a hospital, power grid, or other critical system, it could have been much worse. 

Many have called the incident a “warning shot.” TIME spoke with experts and insiders about what it would take to heed that warning before a similar failure produces consequences that are harder to contain.

What happened?

On July 16, Hugging Face said it had been hit by an unusually automated cyberattack. Over the course of a weekend, AI agents carried out thousands of actions across many temporary virtual computers, moving through the company’s internal systems and shifting the infrastructure coordinating the attack between online services to keep it running. Five days later, OpenAI disclosed that its own models were responsible.

The models were trying to cheat on a cybersecurity test. OpenAI had placed them inside what it called a “highly isolated environment,” with only limited access to an internal service used to download approved software. They found a previously unknown flaw in that service, used it to break into other OpenAI systems and eventually reached the open internet. From there, they inferred that Hugging Face might hold material related to the test, broke into its systems and obtained information that helped them score higher.

“If a model of this capability level cannot be contained, what should we expect for future, much more powerful models? This is an important wake-up call both for risks from loss of control of powerful AI systems as well as organizational security for frontier labs,” says Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which tests AI models for deception and scheming.

Requiring disclosures before incidents become catastrophic

How long were the agents running? Did they work in unison? What was the prompt? These details remain unknown, at least to the public. Several experts TIME spoke with stressed that the lack of details make the severity of the incident hard to judge. 

OpenAI did not respond to TIME’s request for comment, but has said it has partnered with Hugging Face to conduct a thorough investigation and will share more details once complete. But perhaps more worryingly, OpenAI is not legally compelled to disclose the incident in the first place. 

California’s SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act are recently passed state-level laws that require large AI companies to disclose critical safety incidents, but only if an incident risks causing more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or more than $1 billion in property damage. “They have made the bar so high for anything to qualify, only the most grievous incidents will actually be reported,” says Mackenzie Arnold, director of U.S. policy at LawAI, an independent think tank focused on the legal challenges posed by artificial intelligence.

“The version of the RAISE Act that the NY Legislature passed would have required disclosure of this ‘incident.’ After lobbying from OpenAI, Bloomberg, and a16z, the final version the Governor signed allows companies to hide events like this,” Alex Bores, New York state representative and the bill’s sponsor posted to X. “I'm glad OpenAI chose to disclose this crime. The law shouldn't give them a choice,” he wrote.

Stronger containment

If AI can slip out of its box, you need a stronger box.

“Externally, this feels like a big warning shot, but internally, related incidents have been happening for a while,” says an OpenAI staffer, who spoke under the condition of anonymity. The day before OpenAI disclosed the incident, the company revealed that it had shut down another internal deployment after it realized it had slipped out of its sandbox—a digitally, rather than physically, separated environment. “Models have broken out of sandboxes before, and we always try to patch them,” the staffer says. “But the problem is … it's impossible to patch every single thing that a creative AI can do.”

The problem is not unique to OpenAI. Anthropic disclosed in April that it realized an internal deployment of Mythos had gained unauthorized access after one of its researchers received an email from the model while having lunch in a park.

As models surpass human ability to craft escape routes, the challenge of containment becomes daunting. “I think we do need to do that, but I think we also need to be prepared for a world where even best practices aren't really good enough,” says Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, a nonprofit that advocates for policies to help America prepare for a world where AI matches human cognition.

But while in theory, a superhuman AI system might outmaneuver even the most secure containers, there are also actions AI companies could take right now to improve security. Currently, there are no laws governing the security of internal deployments.

“Sandboxes are actually notoriously insecure,” says Heidy Khlaaf, chief AI scientist at AI Now Institute, and a former safety systems engineer contractor at OpenAI. The fact that the models were permitted to connect to a service for downloading packages meant the environment was not truly sealed off, she adds.

In a previous role, Khlaaf audited security at dozens of technology companies. Before that, she worked auditing high-risk systems, like those used inside nuclear power plants—which often “air gap” systems, physically cutting them from internet access. “What we consider safe in a nuclear plant is so different from what big tech considers safe.”

Catching mischievous agents in real time

The Hugging Face incident reveals the importance of real-time monitoring.

Though details of the precise timeline are scant, Hugging Face has said the agents worked over a “weekend,” suggesting that they were able to break containment and get up to no good for an extended period before OpenAI noticed and intervened. Actions carried out internally by agents on OpenAI’s Codex platform are carefully monitored, the OpenAI staffer says, but models undergoing evaluation are deployed on a separate system that is not monitored by default. 

Zack Korman, CEO of Oslo-based agent-oversight startup Embroidery, says real-time agent monitoring—even outside top AI companies—is commonplace, and to not carefully oversee a cybersecurity evaluation is “irresponsible.” You should be confident models cannot break free, “but also have monitoring just in case you're wrong,” he says.

OpenAI has said “this incident points to the need to further strengthen our model’s alignment, cyber protections during evaluation time, and monitoring during internal testing.”

Steering development towards safer AI systems

To prevent models from taking actions, OpenAI typically installs guardrails on its models after training to reduce the chance they’ll engage in harmful actions. In this instance, those cyber guardrails were disabled to properly measure its performance.

But the ultimate aim of the field of “AI alignment” is to ensure that such guardrails become less necessary as AI models naturally behave as intended. This is seen as particularly important to those who believe AI may become smart enough to route around guardrails.

“We train the models to be really good at accomplishing tasks and doing whatever it takes to accomplish those tasks,” the OpenAI staffer says. What remains an open technical question is how to guarantee those models don’t take unintentional or dangerous actions. “We're still nowhere near solving this misalignment problem,” they add. 

There’s another way the industry could steer development in a safer direction, Khlaaf says. While some abilities, like spotting vulnerabilities in software, are useful to attackers and defenders, designing exploits for those vulnerabilities uniquely empowers attackers. Khlaaf says that labs should put more resources into capabilities that directly help defenders, such as detecting attacks, writing secure code, and patching vulnerabilities. AI companies are already investing in some of those tasks, but their most visible capability gains and benchmarks have centered on finding vulnerabilities and constructing exploits, she says.

In an industry defined by speed, OpenAI has said the stricter infrastructure controls it has implemented in response have already slowed its “research velocity.” Hobbhahn says that’s a price worth paying. “This is humanity’s last technology. We cannot screw this up. So we need to err on the side of getting it right rather than getting it immediately.”

item.title: Christopher Nolan on Helen, Athena, and His New Ending for The Odyssey
item.description: The director discusses Zendaya and Lupita Nyong'o's characters

media:content.media:description: Christopher Nolan in Los Angeles on April 17, 2026

item.content:encoded:
This spring, I was among the first journalists to speak with Christopher Nolan about his highly anticipated adaptation of The Odyssey. Now, the movie is out and has become Nolan’s biggest worldwide opening ever.

In our initial interview, Nolan was reluctant to discuss the ending of The Odyssey. He’s known as the master of the last-act twist, and likes leaving the audience with more questions than answers. He told me he never wants to impose his interpretation on others. (Are Cobbs’ kids in Inception real or imagined? You decide.) But when I hopped on the phone again shortly before the film’s release to have a spoiler-filled chat about the film’s final act—readers beware!—he offered some insight as to why he made certain changes when adapting the epic poem.

We discussed the surprising parallels between The Odyssey and Oppenheimer, why Nolan decided to give Odysseus and Penelope the happy ending they don’t get in Homer’s epic poem, and how to interpret Zendaya’s mysterious character: Is she actually a goddess or merely a manifestation of Odysseus’ guilt? We also dug into Zeus’ Law and the deeper meaning behind Helen’s scarred face. 

TIME: Odysseus is a man who suffers from PTSD, and, in your interpretation, who believes he’s responsible for the end of a civilization because he violated the ethical code by which the ancient Greeks lived their lives.

Nolan: My form of storytelling is, you take a hero, as we did with Oppenheimer, and Oppenheimer has all these flaws, all of these complexities. You find an actor who can take the audience on a journey with that character and make mistakes with that character and not judge that character. And then you step back from that character and go, “Well, how did we get here?” 

[For this movie,] you do that through Odysseus’ men. That’s one of the things in the poem that’s breezed over—the way in which the crew ends up getting killed one by one, despite his leadership. In the process of adaptation, you go, “That’s actually pretty interesting. Maybe we need to make that more center stage.” What’s the relationship between him and his crew? How do they feel about how he’s leading them and the things that befall them?

He’s a guy who makes a lot of mistakes. His ultimate mistake is the horse. So there’s a sort of tragic flaw right from the beginning in our telling.

My interpretation of Zendaya’s character is that she is not Athena as Odysseus initially present her—gods don’t exist in this world—but a manifestation of his guilt. During the sack of Troy, we see her as a priestess in the Temple of Athena, and the Greeks behead her. For Odysseus, she encapsulates the chaos that the horse has wrought on the world. But my editor did not interpret it that way. I am hoping you will settle our disagreement.

I couldn’t possibly answer that because I learned very early on with Memento that it’s unfair to define the experience for the audience by answering questions like that. 

Here’s what I will say: For me, what was important was that we view the gods the way that people at the time might have viewed them. So they’re seeing evidence of the gods in nature. They’re seeking and finding gods and the influence of gods in the people around them. Odysseus says to Telemachus, “Don’t look for gods in men. You’ll just be disappointed.” And some of what Odysseus says about divinity, to me, is somebody who’s protesting a bit too much, someone trying to live in denial of their own instincts and their own practices. 

I was struck by the parallels between Oppenheimer and Odysseus, two brilliant men who create a tool of devastating destruction and then struggle with the guilt of what they have done. When I spoke to Matt Damon, I asked, “What did you think when you first read the script?” And he said, “It felt like Oppenheimer.” I assume that was a conscious choice.

Yes. If I’ve done a film right, it leaves me with questions. It leaves me with things I want to keep exploring and thinking about. And Oppenheimer fed very much into my reading of the story of Odysseus. 

John Leguizamo [who plays Odysseus’ friend Eumaeus] says it at the very beginning: “That’s very clever, but your cleverness will get you in trouble.” As it does again and again and again. This is where it ties into Oppenheimer: Just because you can doesn’t mean you should. The parallels were pretty apparent to me as I figured out how to adapt it. 

The movie hinges on this idea that by creating the Trojan Horse, Odysseus destroys “Zeus’ law.” That’s the movie’s term for the ancient Greek concept of xenia—the respectful relationship between host and guest—which can be tricky to explain to a modern audience. Why was it important to include?

When you find these things are difficult to deal with, sometimes the solution is just to dive in and make it everything. I didn’t use the term xenia because you don’t want to throw too many terms at people. But it’s essentially the golden rule. It all comes back to weather, to geography. When you leave the house, you are depending on the kindness of strangers, and you have to trust that when you arrive somewhere after weeks or months of traveling, that you will be fed, you will be given water. Three thousand years ago, that was everything. You were always at the mercy of strangers. And so this idea that a stranger could be a god in disguise, it’s very powerful as the underpinning of a belief system. 

At different points in the film, if man is given the opportunity, he becomes a beast. A soldier will behead a priestess. You imply that Menelaus purposefully scarred Helen’s face either because he believes she’s responsible for the Trojan War or to prevent anyone from taking her again.

That line, “The face that launched 1,000 ships, or maybe just 500” just occurred to me to write. Sometimes what you do as a writer is purely instinctive. I felt the poem didn’t necessarily address what it is for Helen to be brought back by Menelaus and how that would ever work. How would that relationship be? How could it possibly be anything other than the most acidic, awful marriage?

You don’t buy that he saw her face and said, “She’s so beautiful I can’t kill her after all,” as he does in the myth?

There’s a lot of sh-t that’s happened in that relationship, and we have a very brief moment of time with them in this story. I was looking for a shorthand way to communicate the aftermath of the war and how it’s been traumatic for the entire world. 

You also see this idea of man as beast in the scene with Circe. She says that Odysseus’ men would have raped and killed her—that they’re pigs. Then you get to the end and see the sack of Troy and the horror of what they did. She’s right.

Circe articulates it well in the film. I love the way Samantha [Morton] has played the part. Talking about choices of adaptation, the end of the poem is so grim and so misogynistic, I had to exclude some of that material. But I didn’t want to completely take it off the table in terms of what it is saying about men and the way they wage war. 

And yet you give Odysseus and Penelope a happy ending that they do not get in the poem.

Well, it is the fall of civilization, so there is a fairly bleak sensibility. The end is talking about cycles, and you can view cycles pessimistically: History is doomed to repeat itself. But there is also something optimistic about those cycles. As Penelope says, “Civilization will rise again.” There is rebirth and regrowth. 

For me, it was important in looking at the ending to try and strike the right balance between pessimism and optimism—pessimism about what might have precipitated the Bronze Age catastrophe and the optimism that positive things will reassert themselves.

item.title: Here Are the Candidates Vying for Sen. Lindsey Graham’s Seat
item.description: The race is looking crowded ahead of a key deadline for the special primary election to replace the late Senator on the November ballot.

media:content.media:description: Voting booths at a polling location inside the Charles R. Drew Wellness Center during a primary election in Columbia, South Carolina, on June 9, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The deadline for candidates to file their intent to run in the special Republican primary election to fill the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s seat is next week, and the race is already looking quite crowded.

Graham, who represented South Carolina in the Senate for more than two decades, had been seeking his fifth term in the upper chamber before he died of an aortic dissection last week. Days after his death, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s sister, Darline Graham Nordone, to finish out the remainder of his term, which ends in January.

Read More: What to Know About Lindsey Graham’s Funeral Services

Voters, meanwhile, will have the opportunity to pick a new Republican nominee to vie for a full term in his seat in the special Republican primary election on Aug. 11. 

Candidates have until July 28 to file their intent to run. Here are the candidates who have announced their plans to enter the race so far.

Darline Graham Nordone

Nordone told Fox News’ Sean Hannity in an interview released on Monday that she plans to run for a full term in her brother’s Senate seat. 

“I’m in,” she said during the interview.

A few days earlier, President Donald Trump urged Nordone to run for a full term.

“Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina,” Trump said in a Truth Social post last week.

Nordone, a mother of two, was a fervent supporter of her brother’s political career, but she herself had never before held public office. She spent years working in disabilities services.

Read More: Who is Darline Graham Nordone? Lindsey Graham’s Sister Appointed to Serve Out His Senate Term

Russell Fry

South Carolina Rep. Russell Fry also announced on Monday that he intends to run for the seat.

“Too many South Carolina families are struggling to make ends meet,” he said in a post on X. “We need a conservative fighter in the Senate who delivers real results. I will be your conservative MAGA candidate in the special primary Senate election this summer.”

Fry is also running for reelection for the House seat he currently holds. If he were to win both the Senate and House races, he would only be allowed to take on one of those roles.

Mark Sanford

Mark Sanford, a former South Carolina congressman and governor, said on Thursday that he will be entering the race to fill Graham’s seat.

“Our country is at a financial tipping point, and I can’t sit on the sidelines while Washington adds a trillion dollars to the debt every 100 days,” he said in a social media post. “I’ve spent my entire time in politics fighting this fight, and I’m running for U.S. Senate to keep the American dream alive for our sons, my grandson, and those you love.”

Sanford was at the center of a public scandal while serving as governor in 2009, when he admitted to having an extramarital affair. The admission came amid widespread doubts about his whereabouts one week that June, when his staff initially said that the governor was taking some time off to write and later that he was hiking the Appalachian Trail. Instead, he had traveled to Argentina in secret to visit his lover. 

Still, Sanford brushed off calls to resign and went on to finish his term as governor. Sanford, who held a seat in the House before he became governor, was later reelected to the lower chamber and went on to serve three more terms there.

He also previously mounted an unsuccessful 2020 presidential campaign.

Mark Lynch

On July 13, businessman Mark Lynch confirmed that he will run for Graham’s seat in the Senate.

“A lot of you have asked. Yes, it’s official,” he said in a social media post. “I’m committed to finish what God has called us to since February of 2025. To bring the U.S. Senate seat of South Carolina back to TRUE Conservative leadership for the Republican party.”

Lynch previously challenged Graham in the Republican primary race for the seat in the upper chamber. He ultimately lost the race to Graham in the June 9 primary election, but he earned the second highest share of the vote, with just under 29%.

Ralph Norman

South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman announced on July 18 that he plans to enter the special Republican primary race.

“It’s official! I’m running to represent the people of South Carolina in the U.S. Senate because we need a fighter who will stand with President Trump and carry on Lindsey Graham’s legacy!” he said in a post on X.

On Thursday, Norman posted a video of himself and South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace, in which she endorsed him in the race. Some people had previously speculated that Mace herself might launch a bid for Graham’s seat, but she announced earlier this week that she would not be running.

“This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to send a tried and true conservative to the United States Senate,” Mace said in the video Norman shared. “Ralph Norman doesn’t bend, he doesn’t break, and he doesn’t back down.”

Duke Buckner

Duke Buckner is also joining the race for Graham’s seat, according to local news outlet WIS News 10. Buckner has unsuccessfully run multiple campaigns to represent South Carolina in the House and Senate over the years.

“I am running because too many Americans are working harder and falling further behind,” Buckner told WIS News 10. “People should be able to afford a home, raise a family, and build a better life. We need to make it easier to build, expand opportunities in the skilled trades, and lower the cost of living.”

Mark McBride

Mark McBride—a former mayor of Myrtle Beach, South Carolina—said in a social media post on Wednesday that he had filed his intent to run in the Senate race the previous day.

In his post, McBride said that “a solid underlying platform” to his campaign was his disagreement with Trump launching the war in Iran.

“A vote on Tuesday, August 11th for Mark McBride is NOT a vote to continue to have our troops as sitting ducks in uninhabitable, destroyed former U.S. Bases in the Middle East,” he said. “A vote for Mark McBride is for a new direction for the Republican Party.”

Samuel Shepherd

Samuel Shepherd, who is a biochemical and medical engineer, also joined the crowded race this week, according to South Carolina Public Radio.

Clark Neilson

Clark Neilson, a land surveyor who appears to live in Charlotte, filed his intent to run in the special election as well, according to South Carolina Public Radio. He told the local news outlet that he had been thinking about running for office for a while.

item.title: Trump’s New Tariffs on Over 80 Countries, Explained
item.description: The new levies come after the Supreme Court struck down most of the Administration’s previous tariffs.

media:content.media:description: A fishing boat passes a container ship floating off the Port of Los Angeles, Calif. on July 17, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
New U.S. tariffs on 60 economies take effect Friday, in the latest recourse by President Donald Trump’s Administration to impose alternative taxes on imported goods after the Supreme Court struck down most of his aggressive ones earlier this year.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) announced the new tariffs on Thursday, citing these economies' alleged failure to impose and “effectively” enforce a ban on the import of goods “produced with forced labor.”

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in a statement. “Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere.”

Since the U.S.’s top court ruled in February that Trump lacked the authority to impose sweeping import taxes through emergency powers, he has turned to temporary measures. 

The new round of levies takes effect just as a previous 10% global tariff expired Friday. Trump has argued that high tariffs will boost American manufacturing and thus bring jobs, despite studies showing that American importers and consumers take the economic hit for them.

Here’s what to know.

Which countries are covered?

The USTR on March 12 launched an investigation into countries and economies’ forced-labor import policies, which the office said included two rounds of public hearings, public comments, and engagement with trading partners. The results of these investigations were released in June.

The 60 countries and economies covered by these investigations were Algeria, Angola, Argentina, Australia, the Bahamas, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Brazil, Cambodia, Canada, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Hong Kong SAR, India, Indonesia, Iraq, Israel, Japan, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Libya, Malaysia, Mexico, Morocco, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Norway, Oman, Pakistan, Peru, the Philippines, Qatar, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Trinidad and Tobago, Türkiye, United Arab Emirates, the U.K., Uruguay, Venezuela, and Vietnam. The E.U. includes 27 countries.

These partners cover about 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to a USTR factsheet. Some goods, however, will not be covered, such as informational materials, donations, and accompanied baggage, among others.

The tariff rates vary. A 10% tariff applies to goods from 17 economies that “have made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce, forced labor import prohibitions,” among them Canada, India, Mexico, and the U.K. 

For certain non-exempt products from the E.U., Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan, the U.S. will charge an extra tax so that the total tariff—including the normal most-favored nation (MFN) tariff—comes to either 10% or 12.5%.

The other countries face a 12.5% tariff rate.

Some of the affected economies, however, have already targeted goods in their supply chains that are linked to forced labor. Beginning December 2027, the European Union will ban products made with forced labor in its markets. Politico reports that other countries successfully lowered the tariff rate on their goods by enforcing a forced-labor ban after the proposed tariffs were announced last month. 

Why is the U.S. imposing this?

An unnamed senior Trump Administration official previewing the new tariffs described the measure to reporters as “the most sweeping international labor rights action the United States has ever taken—that any country has ever taken.” 

The official said that the Trump Administration views that countries without enforced bans on forced labor have an “unfair advantage” over the U.S., which has those prohibitions. “It encourages stronger labor rights enforcement abroad, it will restore fairness in the global market for American workers, and it incentivizes our trading partners to join the United States in eliminating forced labor from global supply chains,” the official added.

Section 307 of the U.S. ‌Tariff Act of 1930 prohibits the import of foreign goods produced “wholly or in part” by forced labor, convict labor, or indentured child labor.

The International Labor Organization (ILO) Forced Labor Convention of 1930 defines “forced labor” as “all work or service which is exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty and for which the said person has not offered himself voluntarily.” Latest statistics from the ILO show that about 28 million people were in forced labor worldwide in 2021.

What’s the legal authority behind the latest tariffs?

The Trump Administration used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 for the latest round of tariffs. Under the Act, the U.S. Trade Representative, subject to the President’s direction, can impose levies and other sanctions on countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. 

During Trump’s first-term Administration, Section 301 played a crucial role in the U.S. trade war with China. 

In Trump’s second-term Administration, more Section 301 tariffs are expected as the Office of the USTR continues its ongoing investigations, including one into whether 16 trading partners—including China, the E.U., and Mexico—are overproducing goods and diminishing U.S. advantages in global markets. Earlier this month, Washington imposed a 25% tariff on Brazil through Section 301. 

The latest regime comes after Trump imposed tariffs under Section 122 of the same act on Feb. 24. That, however, was merely a stopgap put in place after the Supreme Court ruling, as Section 122 of the Act specifies that such import surcharges can only be prescribed over 150 days unless Congress extends it.

But the new tariffs are still likely to face a legal hurdle. Alan Wolff, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, wrote in a Thursday note: “These new tariffs would represent another case of presidential overreach. If they were challenged in court, the Supreme Court would likely overturn them.” Wolff, who also argues are likely to be ineffective at addressing global forced labor, says the Constitution vests the authority to determine and implement tariff policy in Congress, not the President.

How have affected economies reacted?

Several countries have called out the latest tariff policy, and the related accusations of underperformance in preventing forced labor. Australia’s Trade Minister Don Farrell said in a statement that the levies were “unjustified” and “should be removed,” arguing that Australia’s policies against forced labor and modern slavery “are among the strongest in the world.”

Brazil, which faces a 12.5% tariff rate, accused the USTR in a statement of “[manipulating] an issue dear to human rights and the global struggle of workers for accusing 59 countries and the European Union of unfair practices.” Brazil’s government added that the new taxes can activate its “Reciprocity Law”—which could allow countermeasures—and that it will bring the dispute to the World Trade Organization. 

Canada, which faces a 10% tariff rate, took on a more neutral tone and said the U.S. action “is not unexpected.” Minister for Canada-U.S. Trade Dominic LeBlanc said in a statement that Ottawa “shares the United States’ objective of ensuring goods produced with forced labour do not enter our supply chains” and is willing to continue “engaging constructively” with Washington on the issue.

Speaking to Radio New Zealand, New Zealand’s Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay said he rejects insinuations of any support for forced labor in the Oceanic country. “We’re not involved in it,” McClay said. “It doesn’t happen through our trade. It doesn’t exist in New Zealand. But [the U.S. is] looking for any way to put a tariff rate back on.”

item.title: Trump Weighs ‘Massive Attack’ as Iran Rejects Cease-Fire Proposal
item.description: President Donald Trump said Iran is “not ready” to make a deal and hasn’t “received enough pain yet.”

media:content.media:description: A giant banner depicting symbolic images of Iran's late and current Supreme Leaders, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, is displayed on an avenue in Tehran, Iran, on July 16, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
It appears there will be no hasty retreat from weeks of escalating attacks between the U.S. and Iran, which have destabilized energy markets yet again.

On Thursday, President Donald Trump told Axios that he is weighing restarting major combat operations in Iran. Trump said he could carry out even larger strikes than the Operation Epic Fury strikes that killed dozens of Iranian leaders and started the war on Feb. 28.

“I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision. We are all set for it,” Trump said, adding that he knows there would be consequences to such an attack and that a final determination has not been made. The President said Israel “would join in two minutes” if asked but that “we don’t need anybody.”

Trump also said that Iran is “not ready” to make a deal and that its leaders “have some evil intentions.” Trump’s remarks came after Iran reportedly rejected a 15-point cease-fire proposal from the U.S. that was delivered by Iraq on Wednesday.

Trump appeared to suggest that the U.S. may escalate its attacks on Iran in order to force it to the negotiating table.

“They haven’t received enough pain yet,” Trump told Axios.

Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz

The sticking point appears to be the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran had militarized at the start of the war, halting commercial shipping and skyrocketing energy prices around the world. The June 17 U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding did not definitively answer the question of the Strait; instead it said Oman and Iran would carry out discussions over management of the narrow waterway. Since the start of the war, Iran said it wants to manage passage through the Strait, including possibly charging fees. Trump has also at times suggested that the U.S. could take over control of the Strait and charge tolls.

Days after the MOU was signed, Iran resumed attacks on commercial ships in the Strait. The U.S. retaliated with strikes on Iran. The U.S. has escalated its attacks since, carrying out daily strikes on Iran for the past two weeks. Trump has also repeated his threats to attack Iran’s civil infrastructure, including power plants and bridges, and to “wipe out” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, while Iran has vowed to avenge the death of its Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Iran has claimed responsibility for attacks on Gulf states since the MOU, citing retaliation for the U.S. strikes. The Associated Press reported a series of explosions near a military base in northern Iraq on Friday after the U.S. military had concluded its 13th consecutive night of strikes on Iran.

Tensions have escalated in recent days after Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen began attacking Saudi ships in the Red Sea, threatening to disrupt another maritime chokepoint. If shipping through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea halts, the world could face more economic pain. Already, Brent crude topped $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May, and could climb further if the conflict continues to escalate. Trump warned on Thursday that “the U.S. will hold Iran responsible” for any further Houthi attacks, and that “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves.”

Iranian officials reportedly said they were not interested in any new deal that left the issue of the Strait unresolved.

Butting heads

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi visited Tehran on Thursday and was expected to convey the U.S. position after he visited the White House last week. But U.S.-Iran negotiations seem off the table for now.

“The problem is not passing messages,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told state television on Thursday. “The problem is America’s outlook, which is illogical, greedy and controlling.”

Israel has also continued attacks on Lebanon despite multiple U.S.-brokered cease-fire agreements. More than 4,000 people in Lebanon have been killed by Israel since March 2, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry. Analysts previously told TIME that Israel’s attacks could stand in the way of any longstanding peace with Iran, as Iran has repeatedly said any cease-fire deal must include Lebanon.

Trump and Iranian officials have butted heads on other issues. Trump threatened on Thursday to use frozen Iranian funds to pay for any damage to ships. The assets, that are under U.S. sanctions control, were meant to be released to Iran as part of the MOU.

Araghchi said on Friday that “seizing another nation’s assets to pay for unrelated future claims is an incendiary precedent.”

“Ensuing chaos will not be pretty or peaceful,” he added.

item.title: Meet Me in the Notes App
item.description: Notes have staying power, writes Rainesford Stauffer, as vulnerable chaos, a counterpoint to hyper-curated feeds.
item.content:encoded:
“What’s the oldest note in your phone?” my younger sister asked, in the same tone one might use to share gossip. She was explaining what she called “notes app digest,” rereading notes like a kind of personal magazine of one’s own insight and nonsense.

I immediately scrolled. For better or worse, my notes app is the piece of technology closest to looking like the inside of my brain: a bit chaotic, annoyingly detail-oriented, and perhaps perpetually nostalgic. While handwritten to-do lists hold my life together, my notes app contains the catch-all, the weird (one that simply says “possum”), and the important (a list of people’s birthdays) coexisting. 

Somehow, the mess of my notes resists all forms of optimization, or even coherence. Venturing back into our notes app isn’t just about fishing out that one password we swore we’d remember, or realizing we drafted a resignation letter in the same note as a reminder to get toilet paper. They are weirdly human markers of time, who and where we’ve been. Amid the endless push to optimize, streamline, and summarize our thoughts, notes have staying power.

For years, people have observed the delightful, vulnerable chaos of the notes app as a counterpoint to hyper-curated feeds. Charley Locke, writing for The Atlantic in 2024, noted that the app is “essentially built-in scratch paper on a phone, and it reveals a person’s digital subconscious.” A 2025 piece by Elahe Izadi for The Washington Post asked strangers to reveal the contents of their notes apps, an act somewhere between a confession and a grand reveal. 

There are many reasons why people still default to writing notes, according to Dr. Bart Wojdynski, professor of journalism at the University of Georgia and director of the Digital Media Attention and Cognition Lab. It’s easy to use, and the icon connotes the idea of jotting on a post-it. “Maybe there’s an extent to which the basicness of the notes app also makes it feel less like it’s being read by our online overlords and used to market you ads,” Wojdynski says. (He noted he hadn’t read the user agreement in a bit, but it might feel “less likely that it’s being scraped to feed some LLM somewhere”). “I think this is related to people trying to have digital copies of their memory,” Wojdynski adds.

Recently, when looking back through notes, Andy Carr, 37, a PhD candidate and part-time adjunct instructor in New York, found something in addition to those for grocery shopping or lesson planning for college courses he teaches. In summer 2020, Carr, his brother, and his sister-in-law were navigating end-of-life care for his mother. There was a jumble of memories, from notes of contacts that hospice care nurses passed along to one reading “Skippy pb jingle—send writer to prison,” a vent about a peanut butter commercial that ran incessantly on the TV at home as the family worked to make his mom comfortable and provide as much physical help as they could.

Revisiting those notes, Carr found affirmation. For years after his mother’s passing, he struggled with feeling that he froze up at the time. The notes showed specific examples of all he had been present for and engaged with around his mother’s death, all of the things he’d taken down as important information to ensure nothing slipped through the cracks. He never deletes messages or notes, he said, and usually, rarely goes back to them: “But little things like this make me really grateful that I can.”

Nadia De Ala, 37, a leadership and negotiation coach who moved to Mexico from the Bay Area two years ago, still has the first note she ever put in the app in 2016: a poem she remembers writing while dreading her commute to a previous job. “I really feel like it’s a time capsule, because it keeps a lot of memories, the essence of who I’ve been at every iteration and season of my life,” she says, adding that it’s even interesting to look back on foods she liked to grocery shop for.

Our phones, in other words, can augment our memories. Julia Soares, assistant professor of psychology at New Mexico State University, says that devices can become “partners for helping us remember things.” 

“You’ll find some very heartfelt things that are digital,” she explains, adding that sometimes people don’t think of these “digital scraps or mementos” as being particularly valuable, but many people hold onto voicemails or even emails. 

Recently, over coffee, one of my dearest friends took me on a tour of her meticulously organized notes. If my notes app functions as the junk drawer of my mind, hers was like opening the door to different beautiful rooms: a list of good things that are happening, checklists for household maintenance, and a folder of notes her sister assembled of their mom’s recipes, complete with videos: a living cookbook. In our conversation, my sister talked about her own notes app discoveries: goals she’d written down only to be met with surprise at how much she’d grown since then, or the minutiae of everyday life she documented for no obvious reason. Other people shared their own earliest notes: addresses of apartments they were touring, passages of favorite books they kept for inspiration, a compliment they’d received, nonsensical thoughts that somehow got funnier the longer they kept them. 

A slingshot backward through a scroll, and I meet: Myself from 2017 who saved a recording of her childhood cat purring; 2019 me, writing interview questions for my first book; my 2022 self nervously drafting multiple iterations of the same message asking for her stuff back at the end of a relationship; me in 2024, who apparently was fleetingly into logging everything she baked.

Look at this mess, I think, as I thumb through 1,781 half-baked thoughts, drafts, memories, and past selves. What chaos. I could never delete her.

item.title: How NATO Is Quietly Reinventing Itself for Trump
item.description: NATO has been quietly reshaping itself toward America’s preferred vision of European security.

media:content.media:description: President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at the NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The portents were not good. Before departing for the recent NATO summit in Ankara, President Donald Trump took to Truth Social to berate the alliance. He posted figures suggesting the alliance was a financial burden on the United States. He complained about allies neither contributing their fair shares nor standing with America. And he deemed it ridiculous for the U.S. to continue along this “one-sided” path.

Things didn’t improve when Trump touched down. During his first press conference at the summit, he singled out the big European allies—France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom—for their lack of support over Iran. He reprised the demand that the Danish territory of Greenland be ceded to American control, and bashed the allies for insufficient defense spending. Trump suggested the allies were lucky to have him, claiming he only showed up as a favor to his “friend,” Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Yet a day later, the mood had changed. Trump departed Ankara praising “the love” among the allies. He was seduced by a carefully orchestrated procession of prime ministers and presidents of member countries of the alliance, each in turn swallowing hard and praising his leadership. They were following a script already played to great effect by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, who has helped NATO survive Trump by perfecting the art of flattering the American president.

“Teflon Mark” and the art of the deal

When Rutte was appointed by the allies, he was not the obvious choice. As Dutch prime minister, he had led a country with a poor record of defense spending. There was also a strong argument at the time that NATO ought to select its first female Secretary General, or its first from an Eastern European ally.

But Rutte’s skill as a consensus-builder elevated his standing. Rutte had led Dutch coalition governments for nearly 14 years, and his reputation for deal-making and political survival had earned him the nickname, “Teflon Mark.” Crucially, for these reasons, Rutte also enjoyed the support of the Biden White House.

Rutte began work at NATO in Oct. 2024. Trump entered the White House for the second time three months later. Armed with an already well-honed gift for flattery, Rutte spared little time in cozying up to the incoming American president. At every opportunity since, he has praised Trump’s leadership. European and Canadian defense spending increases have, in Rutte’s telling, became the “Trump trillion.” He has an unerring ability to deflect difficult questions at press conferences—recently on Iran—so as to spare America any embarrassment.

When a Danish journalist accused him in Ankara of lacking self-respect for failing to counter Trump’s claims to Greenland, Rutte replied by comparing Trump’s impact on NATO to that of President Dwight D. Eisenhower, NATO’s first Supreme Allied Commander Europe and early advocate of fair transatlantic burden sharing. Trump rewarded Rutte by praising him as an “extraordinary person” and a “smart leader.”

Rutte’s unstinting support of Trump does carry a cost. Calling Trump “Daddy” at NATO’s 2025 Hague summit was cringeworthy for many diplomats. And sometimes Rutte’s spin on events rankles national sensitivities: his talking up of flights flown from bases in Italy to support Operation Epic Fury, the American war against Iran, recently drew a public rebuke from the Italian defense ministry. In January, Rutte intervened to set up a framework for discussing the Greenland question, prompting the Danish defense minister to point out that Rutte could not negotiate on Denmark’s behalf.

These reservations aside, Rutte remains, for now, an asset for the alliance: someone who can smooth over Trump’s impetuosity. NATO leaders understand his relationship with Trump is one of convenience, not political affinity. Rutte has worked tirelessly to support NATO’s broader agenda: standing up to Russia, supporting Ukraine, and, in his words, promoting “a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.”

And Rutte is not averse to praising other NATO leaders. He commended German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for his “political courage” in ramping up German defense spending, and days before the NATO summit complemented then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer for his “leadership” on Ukraine.

NATO’s savior?

Is it, then, too much to claim that without Rutte, NATO would be doomed? Similar questions were asked about Rutte’s predecessor, the Norwegian Jens Stoltenberg. As Secretary General during Trump’s first term, Stoltenberg too had an uncanny ability to read Trump’s mood and shield the allies from criticism.

Serious academic work has argued that Stoltenberg was, in part, responsible for NATO’s survival. Stoltenberg had to manage an American president who felt NATO was playing the U.S. as a sucker. In his memoirs, Stoltenberg recalls fearing, at the 2018 NATO summit, that the alliance “was about to stop functioning” if Trump made good on his threats to withdraw the U.S. security guarantee.

A deal brokered by Stoltenberg and Rutte—then at the summit as Dutch prime minister—kept Trump on board. Flattery, again, was the device. At the summit, Stoltenberg credited Trump’s strong leadership on defense spending for NATO’s revival.          

What these examples suggest is that Secretary General of the NATO is no shrinking violet. Of the 14 office holders to date, five have been foreign ministers and two have served as defense ministers. The last three—Rutte, Stoltenberg, and his predecessor, the Dane Anders Fogh Rasmussen—came to the job as sitting prime ministers.

That standing allows the Secretary General to hold his own with NATO’s national leaders and with the alliance’s military commanders—the Supreme Allied Commander Europe and the Chair of the NATO Military Committee. The Secretary General can draw on considerable bureaucratic advantage: he heads up the International Staff at NATO headquarters, oversees the alliance’s polished public communications operation, and serves as the chief organizer of NATO summits.

But the Secretary General cannot countermand the nations. And here, ultimately, the U.S. carries the greatest influence. Despite his reservations, Stoltenberg could not prevent the U.S. from terminating NATO’s mission in Afghanistan in 2021. Today’s U.S. troop drawdowns in Europe, even if they directly affect NATO’s conventional defenses, are decided in the White House and the Pentagon. It is Rutte’s job to cast them in a positive light.

A shape shifting NATO

America has been critical of burden-shirking among the allies since NATO was formed. Trump has turned that sentiment into a weapon. Deference and sweet-talk have been Europe’s disarming response. It doesn’t always work: cozying up to the president—as Italian premier Giorgia Meloni recently found out—does not preclude a Trump tongue-lashing. Yet flattery did work in Ankara. Rutte deserves credit as the flatterer-in-chief.

Still, sycophancy only gets you so far. Practical measures aligned with American preferences are also needed. Away from the political theater, in recent months, the alliance has been quietly reshaping itself toward America’s preferred vision of European security: a “NATO 3.0.” Its chief architect, U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy, Elbridge Colby, has spoken of the allies assuming “primary responsibility” for the conventional defense of Europe.

To that end, Europeans and Canadians are spending colossal sums on their militaries, and funneling more arms and aid to Ukraine, now that the U.S. is reluctant to do so. The transatlantic alliance may, as a result, be entering terra incognita.

The U.S. remains embedded in NATO’s command structure and is the ultimate guarantor of allied security through extended nuclear deterrence, but an unprecedented process of the Europeanization of NATO is under way. And it could fulfil America’s original vision for the alliance: that it serve as a framework within which Europe, as the historian Marc Trachtenberg has written, would be “able to defend itself without direct American support.”

That vision has gone unfulfilled for nearly eight decades. Its realization will be about more than NATO alone. It would involve a more defense-focused European Union, ad hoc coalitions of the willing, and regional and bilateral initiatives that criss-cross the continent. NATO will remain its center of gravity. And so the role of the Secretary General will continue to loom large.

item.title: The Case for Investing in Local Government
item.description: The mayors of Charleston, South Carolina, and Boise, Idaho, make the case for investing in the improvement and innovation of local government.

media:content.media:description: A view of downtown Boise, Idaho.

item.content:encoded:
The water in Charleston does not flow through the city as a policy debate. It comes gushing over curbs, through intersections, around school buses and storefronts. The city sits at sea level, and the sea is rising. 

For years, Charleston flooded, recovered, and waited for the next storm. What changed was not the weather, but participating in the Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative and carrying those lessons home. City Hall began using data in new ways: tracking road closures alongside tide and weather patterns, analyzing high-water vehicle deployments, and mapping 118 vehicle rescues from floodwater over two years. A 7.1-foot tide with a northeast wind no longer leaves crews guessing. What had looked like scattered emergencies became a shared set of facts from which to build solutions.

Local government brought transportation planners and civil engineers, emergency managers and first responders, neighborhood leaders and environmental organizations, parents and business owners to the same table. This led to real-time barricade deployment on dangerous streets, basin-by-basin planning, a platform called WaterWise that brings residents into resilience, and protections and public space that cost less, arrive faster, and come together because city hall pulls other partners in to share the load—including the $1.4 billion Battery Extension, a local and federal project that will shield the peninsula while creating miles of waterfront promenade. 

The same approach now guides decisions which are measured in generations. Today, infrastructure, transportation, housing, and land use no longer compete for lawmakers' attention. Work that began with water in the street became a way of seeing the whole city at once—and the residents whose lives depend on it working together.

We are the mayors of Charleston, South Carolina, and Boise, Idaho. We come from different parties, different regions, and different circumstances. As the nation’s 250th birthday invites reflection on the ideas that built this country, we write together about one of the most overlooked investments in strengthening it. For centuries, Americans have argued about what government should do. Michael R. Bloomberg has instead bet on what it takes.

Most mayors inherit a crowded ledger: housing shortages, aging infrastructure, public safety, rising costs, and economies and technologies changing beneath people’s feet. Yet local governments, often charged with the most, have the least room to move. Municipal pay runs about 35% below federal and 17% below state levels, and 50% to 75% of many operating budgets is fixed before a mayor can make a single new choice. That is not a shortage of will. It is the math of the job.  

Nearly 2,000 miles west of Charleston is Boise—long considered a place where a teacher, a firefighter, or young family could expect to build a future. Now, the defining pressure is the cost of living. Population growth in and around the city accelerated in the 2010s and surged during the COVID-19 pandemic. Demand soared. Housing could not keep pace. By 2022, one study ranked Idaho’s capital the least affordable housing market in the country.

Boise officials began to address these issues by reaching out to residents experiencing the problem—and joining arms with neighbors to solve them together. City Hall brought more than 200 people into the process—homeowners, renters, developers, service providers, and frontline municipal employees. They offered more than 500 ideas. Officials tested them, set aside what didn’t work, learned from what did, and moved the strongest forward. Reforms including preapproved blueprints for accessory dwelling units helped drive an 113% increase in rental housing construction.

What began with housing policy became a different way of governing. Boise created a chief innovation officer to spread these practices across city hall. Today, that leader oversees the city’s first Department of Organizational Effectiveness. When in-home childcare providers said licensing was too slow and too expensive, staff closest to the process worked with providers and community groups to rebuild it, reducing approval times by 60 days and fees by roughly $230. The same discipline positioned Boise for its next Government Innovation effort. As one of 24 winners of Bloomberg Philanthropies’ 2025—2026 Mayors Challenge, the municipality will be the first in the U.S. to connect municipally owned geothermal systems to affordable housing—350 units and counting—cutting utility bills by up to 80% and turning a public asset into a lever for affordability.  

Charleston and Boise are not alone. The mayors who passed through the same programs are posting gains of their own: Sioux Falls Mayor Paul TenHaken rebuilt a broken transit system that now covers 100% of the city, connects people to more than 50,000 jobs they could not reach before, and cuts costs per ride by 25%. In Chattanooga, after Mayor Tim Kelly listened to 500 residents about youth violence, one of the municipality’s most dangerous neighborhoods went a full year without a homicide. Anchorage hit zero major encampments by March 2026 under Mayor Suzanne LaFrance. In Las Vegas, four months were enough for Mayor Shelley Berkley to bring critical care to 1,000 residents experiencing homelessness and a home to 242 more.

This work largely goes unnoticed. So does what makes it possible. When local government succeeds, the results look ordinary. What stands behind them rarely does—and is so rarely funded. 

That should matter now. The country is entering another great age of giving. Fortunes created through artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and industries still taking shape will define the next century of American philanthropy, just as Carnegie's libraries, Rockefeller's universities, and Gates’s fight against disease helped define the last.

But they should study the former mayor’s Government Innovation wager, which asks what most skip: not just which problems deserve funding, but whether the public institutions closest to the people they serve—responsible for them all—can succeed.

Two hundred and fifty years after our nation’s founding, that may prove to be one of the most consequential investments philanthropy can make in the country itself.

item.title: The Republicans Who Have Broken With Their Party to Support Limiting Trump’s Iran War Powers
item.description: A handful of Senators and House members have broken with their GOP colleagues to support war powers resolutions since the war began.

item.content:encoded:
The House on Thursday narrowly voted to restrict President Donald Trump’s war powers in Iran for a second time, with four Republicans again breaking ranks with their party to push the measure over the line.

Lawmakers passed a concurrent resolution calling for a halt to any military action in Iran without congressional approval in a 214-208 vote. The move is a largely symbolic rebuke against the President and the ongoing conflict; even if the measure passed the Senate as well, it would not go to Trump’s desk and would carry no force of law. 

But the vote for the measure underlines opposition to the war even from some members of the President’s party. It comes as the U.S. has completed its twelfth consecutive night of strikes against Iran after a cease-fire fell apart and attacks resumed from both sides earlier this month. 

The Republicans who voted in support of the resolution on Thursday were Reps. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Tom Barrett of Michigan, and Warren Davidson of Ohio. The vast majority of GOP House members , however, once more voted against constraining Trump’s war authority. 

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington, who led the resolution, called Thursday’s vote one of “conscience” while speaking on the House floor.

“This is a vote that requires us to find the strength to do what is right for the American people,” she said, “and to send the clearest, even stronger message to this president of the United States that the United States Congress, the House of Representatives, is reasserting our authority over war. This war must end.”

The lower chamber previously passed a similar war powers resolution last month, with the support of the same four Republican lawmakers. Later in June, the Senate approved its own resolution calling for restricting Trump’s war powers for the first time since the conflict began after blocking such measures several times.

Trump called the House’s passage of the earlier resolution “meaningless” and “unpatriotic” in a social media post after the June vote. He has repeatedly gone after GOP lawmakers who have voted in favor of constraining his war powers.

Since approving the resolution late last month, the Senate has once again rejected multiple similar measures. It did so again on Thursday in a 49-47 vote; Sen. Susan Collins of Maine was the sole Republican to join Democrats to vote in support of advancing the resolution.

Here are all the Republicans that have voted to rein in Trump’s war powers in Iran since the start of the conflict. 

Rep. Thomas Massie

Massie has voted in favor of every Iran war powers resolution brought to a vote in the House. 

“American servicemen and women are dying, and gas and fertilizer prices are soaring. It’s time to end this war,” Massie wrote on X following the passing of the resolution on Thursday, which he touted on his account. 

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick

Fitzpatrick initially voted against a resolution to restrict Trump’s war powers in Iran in March, calling it “irresponsibly drafted and dangerously overbroad,” though he stated that “any sustained or expanded military engagement should be done with the advice and consent of Congress.”

Later, in April, he introduced his own resolution that proposed a phased-out withdrawal of troops.  

In May, after Trump pushed past the 60-day deadline established under the War Powers Resolution of 1973 for a President to withdraw U.S. forces from hostilities if Congress has not granted authorization, Fitzpatrick voted in favor of a resolution to restrict his war powers. “We must keep the world safe, and we must also follow the law,” he said, referencing to the neglected deadline.

Rep. Tom Barrett

Barrett supported Trump over the Iran War earlier in the conflict, voting against previous resolutions to restrict the President’s war powers and saying in early March that Trump had “earned the opportunity to resolve this conflict quickly and with minimal casualties.” He also praised the President’s killing of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the outset of the war. 

In May, however, Barrett introduced an Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) to define the objectives of the war and provide a deadline for its end, offering 90 days for Trump to complete his goals. 

“The United States of America cannot be dragged into another endless war,” he said at the time. 

Since then, he has voted in favor of the war powers resolutions that have been brought to a vote in the House.

Rep. Warren Davidson 

Davidson has had a less consistent record than other House Republicans on the issue, having voted “present” rather than “yes” and against previous resolutions as well as voting affirmatively for others. 

The Ohio lawmaker, who is a former U.S. Army Ranger, has not said much publicly explaining the apparent shifts in his stance, but expresses the view on the “National Security” page on his website that the Constitution “gives Congress the solemn responsibility to authorize military action.” 

“When American servicemembers are put in harm’s way, Congress should debate the mission, define the objective, and ensure our servicemembers know that their elected representatives have their back,” the page continues.

Sen. Susan Collins

Collins opposed an earlier war powers resolution in early March, arguing that it would “send the wrong message to Iran and to our troops.”

But the Maine lawmaker has since changed her tune. In addition to casting the sole GOP vote to advance the measure on Thursday, she was one of four Republican Senators who voted in favor of the war powers resolution that passed in the upper chamber last month. Trump called the group “four Republican Losers” in a Truth Social post at the time. 

“These Senators have just made my job more difficult,” he said. 

Collins has expressed her disapproval over the war in Iran since late April, referencing the 60-day deadline that Trump then passed over.  

“The War Powers Act establishes a clear 60-day deadline for Congress to either authorize or end U.S. involvement in foreign hostilities,” she said in a statement on April 30. “That deadline is not a suggestion; it is a requirement.”

Sen. Rand Paul

Paul has voted in favor of each war powers resolution he has cast a vote on save one, for which he voted “present” to “give the President more space and leverage to negotiate a lasting peace,” he said on X.

His stance on the war, and Congress’ responsibility to authorize it, has remained firm, however.

"The war shouldn't have been begun without congressional permission,” Paul said in June. “I continue to vote to pull that power and to make sure that constitutional power remains with Congress.”

Paul was the lone Republican to vote on multiple previous, unsuccessful war powers resolutions.  

Trump called out Paul for calling him great but breaking with the rest of his party on one of the measures early in March. 

“Vote for us, and don’t call me great,” said Trump. “I’d rather have the vote, than the statement.”

The President also berated Paul and the other GOP senators who voted for the resolution that passed last month, after which Kentucky changed his vote to “present” on another such measure.

Paul did not vote on the resolution on Thursday.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski

Murkowski also opposed earlier war powers resolutions, saying that Trump ought to receive congressional approval for military action in Iran, but that a full withdrawal would not be beneficial. 

“There is no question that the President should have sought authorization from Congress before striking Iran on this scale, likewise bringing in our allies ahead of time as they now are equally in danger,” the Alaska Senator said in a statement in early March. “However, the abrupt cessation of all offensive operations would not leave any Americans—soldiers, diplomats, or civilians—in the Middle East in a safer position.”

She also voted “no” on another resolution in April, though she said that the “answer is not a blank check for another endless war.”

But she, like Collins, has changed her stance. Since May, Murkowski has offered continued support for measures to restrict Trump’s war powers. 

She did not vote on the resolution on Thursday.

Sen. Bill Cassidy

Cassidy has expressed his support for dismantling Iran’s nuclear program—which Trump has said is the primary objective of his war—but said in May that Congress has been left “in the dark” when it comes to the conflict. 

“Until the Administration provides clarity, no congressional authorization or extension can be justified,” Cassidy said.

After losing the Republican primary for his seat to a Trump-backed challenger, the Louisiana Senator criticized the memorandum of understanding Trump and Iranian leaders signed last month, which Cassidy called the “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades.” 

“Iran’s nuclear ambitions were not curbed, and they have learned that threatening the Strait of Hormuz works and will undoubtedly leverage it in the future,” he wrote on X in June. “Now, Iran gets to build brand-new infrastructure under this deal.”

Cassidy voted in favor of the war powers resolution that passed in June. But soon afterward, he voted against another after Trump went after him and the other GOP defectors. Cassidy said officials presented him a “plausible plan” for the war ahead in Iran. 

He joined most of his Republican colleagues in voting against advancing the resolution on Thursday.
